name: Un F-94 engancha con su radar un blanco que el radar de tierra le había señalado en la cola y lo ve alejarse de 6.000 a unas 26.000 yardas en unos 14 segundos, tras hacer pasadas a una luz sin contorno · posible avería del radar para las FEAF (Corea del Sur, 1952)
name_en: An F-94 locks its radar on a target the ground radar had reported on its tail and watches it pull away from 6,000 to about 26,000 yards in about 14 seconds, after making passes at a light with no outline · possible radar malfunction for FEAF (South Korea, 1952)

location.place: Sector de Chorwon (hoy Cheorwon, Corea del Sur), detrás de las líneas de la ONU: cuadrícula militar CT 3930 del informe, convertida a coordenadas por cálculo propio y aproximada; la luz estaba en CT 5050, unos 22 km al nornordeste, más allá de la línea de bombardeo, en lo que hoy es Corea del Norte
location.place_en: Chorwon sector (today Cheorwon, South Korea), behind the UN lines: the report's military grid square CT 3930, converted to coordinates by our own calculation and approximate; the light was at CT 5050, some 22 km to the north-northeast, beyond the bomb line, in what is today North Korea

summary: En la madrugada del 26 de mayo de 1952, un caza nocturno F-94 del 319.º Escuadrón de Caza-Interceptación que patrullaba el sector central del frente de Corea hizo unas siete pasadas, hasta 50 pies, a una luz brillante en la que no distinguió contorno. Después el radar de tierra «Bromide» le avisó de algo en la cola, y hacia las 03:20 el operador de radar del caza lo enganchó a 7.000 yardas, y a partir de 6.000 el blanco se alejó hasta unas 24.000 a 26.000 yardas en unos 14 segundos, sin que nadie lo viera con claridad, mientras el F-94 encendía la poscombustión. Piloto y operador firmaron sus declaraciones; la inteligencia de las FEAF calculó unos 5.580 nudos y lo atribuyó a una posible avería del radar de a bordo. La tarjeta de Blue Book marca «Possibly Balloon».
summary_en: In the early hours of 26 May 1952, an F-94 night fighter of the 319th Fighter-Interceptor Squadron patrolling the central sector of the Korean front made some seven passes, down to 50 feet, at a brilliant light in which it could make out no outline. Then the "Bromide" ground radar warned it of something on its tail, and at about 0320 the fighter's radar operator locked on to it at 7,000 yards, and from 6,000 the target drew away to about 24,000 to 26,000 yards in about 14 seconds, without anyone seeing it clearly, while the F-94 lit its afterburner. Pilot and operator signed statements; FEAF intelligence computed about 5,580 knots and put it down to a possible malfunction of the airborne radar. The Blue Book record card ticks "Possibly Balloon".

whatHappened:
En la madrugada del lunes 26 de mayo de 1952, un caza nocturno F-94 del 319.º Escuadrón de Caza-Interceptación, que había despegado de la base K-13 (Suwon) en una patrulla aérea de combate, volaba sobre el sector central del frente de Corea. El controlador de interceptación de tierra, con indicativo «Bromide», le avisó de un desconocido en la cuadrícula militar CT 4856 y le pidió que lo investigara. Según la declaración del piloto, bajaron a unos 2.500 pies y vieron, a la luz de los reflectores de primera línea, una avioneta por debajo de ellos, pero el terreno no les dejó descender más para identificarla. Bromide les dijo que la dejaran y tomaran rumbo sur.

Al girar vieron un objeto brillante por encima y por delante. Con permiso de Bromide hicieron una primera pasada de norte a sur a unos 600 pies y luego una serie de pasadas desde los cuatro puntos cardinales, hasta unos 50 pies, sin distinguir ningún contorno por el brillo de la luz. El operador de radar, cuyo nombre está tachado, cuenta lo mismo con otros detalles: el piloto, al que llama «Martin», fue quien vio la luz; él no consiguió captarla en su radar, aunque el controlador decía que la estaba detectando en su pantalla («I can not understand how GCI was painting this target and I could not pick it up»); hicieron unas siete pasadas, y cuando sacó la cabeza del visor le pareció «a bright blue light».

Las dos declaraciones cuentan en distinto orden lo que pasó después. Según el operador, tras la última pasada, a unos 7.000 pies, Bromide anunció que tenían algo en la cola; él se volvió y creyó ver un avión, sin poder asegurarlo, porque fue un segundo. Según el piloto, fue el operador quien, en la última pasada, miró atrás y dijo que creía ver un objeto en la cola, y él no le dio mucho crédito hasta que Bromide llamó para decir que detectaba en su pantalla algo detrás del caza. El piloto pidió un vector de interceptación y, con la luz todavía a la vista, viró a estribor. Con rumbo nordeste, el operador enganchó un blanco con el radar de a bordo, un APG-33, a 7.000 yardas, casi de frente y un poco por encima, y el caza empezó a acercarse a 50 nudos más que él. A 6.000 yardas el blanco empezó a alejarse. El piloto encendió la poscombustión, desde unos 250 nudos, y siguió al blanco en una subida suave, por encima de los 10.000 pies, con el eco casi centrado en la pantalla, mientras la distancia crecía a ritmo constante: hasta unas 26.000 yardas en 12 a 15 segundos, según el piloto, o unas 24.000 en unos 14, según el operador. Ahí se perdió el enganche, y no volvieron a captarlo en el resto de la misión. Ninguno de los dos vio maniobras evasivas ni estela de escape. El operador añadió: «I believe that this was the target GCI was painting all the time, and that he was in our area while we were making passes at the light».

Al día siguiente el resumen de inteligencia de la Quinta Fuerza Aérea recogió los dos episodios por separado: a las 03:20, en CT 3930 y a 7.500 pies, la persecución por radar de un «unidentified aircraft»; a las 03:25, en CT 5050 y a 7.000 pies, un «unidentified aircraft» con una luz muy fuerte, visible a más de 5 millas, que según la tripulación «definitely» no era un globo, porque habían pasado justo por debajo a 50 pies; «No outline was visible because of the brilliant light». Esas horas invierten el orden de las declaraciones, que ponen la luz antes de la persecución. El 29 de mayo los dos tripulantes firmaron sus declaraciones (la del piloto, ante el capitán Fielder C. Slingluff III; en la del operador, el nombre del testigo está tachado), y el 31 el capitán Vincent A. Goskey, del Destacamento 1 del 6004.º Escuadrón de Servicio de Inteligencia Aérea, envió el informe 52-85 con las respuestas al cuestionario que había mandado la inteligencia de las Fuerzas Aéreas del Lejano Oriente (FEAF): el radar se comprobaba antes y después de cada misión y funcionaba «very good»; el operador no apartó la vista de la pantalla; el tiempo se midió contando en voz alta, con un error que el informe da por no mayor de dos segundos por minuto. El informe dice también, del blanco de radar, que «no actual ascertainable visual observation was made», y de la luz, que solo hubo contacto visual. Alguien anotó un «?» al margen de esas dos frases subrayadas. La página 2 de ese informe de cuatro no está en el expediente, y en las páginas 7 y 8 del extracto de las FEAF una mano escribió «Where's the rest of the report?».

El general de brigada Charles Y. Banfill, responsable de inteligencia de las FEAF (Deputy for Intelligence), hizo la cuenta: unos 68.500 pies recorridos, una aceleración de 650 pies por segundo al cuadrado, unas 20 g, y una velocidad final de unos 5.580 nudos; aunque el cronometraje o la calibración se desviaran un 50 %, seguiría por encima de cualquier misil conocido. Añadió que el controlador de Bromide aún no había enviado nada sobre los ecos que registró, y concluyó que esa aceleración llevaba a creer que el APG-33 no funcionaba bien en el momento del contacto, pese a las comprobaciones. La tarjeta de Blue Book resume el caso como «Ground Radar, Air Radar, Air Visual Combined Sightings», da como solución una posible avería del radar de a bordo y marca «Possibly Balloon», con «Was Aircraft», «Probably Aircraft» y «Unknown» tachados; el índice de Blue Book de 1952 lo lista como «BALLOON WITH FLARE».
whatHappened_en:
In the early hours of Monday 26 May 1952, an F-94 night fighter of the 319th Fighter-Interceptor Squadron, which had taken off from K-13 (Suwon) on a combat air patrol, was flying over the central sector of the Korean front. The ground-controlled intercept controller, call sign "Bromide", told the crew about an unknown in military grid square CT 4856 and asked them to investigate. According to the pilot's statement, they came down to about 2,500 feet and saw, in the glare of the front-line searchlights, a small plane below them, but the terrain kept them from descending further to identify it. Bromide told them to drop it and take up a southerly heading.

As they turned they saw a brilliant object above and ahead. With Bromide's permission they made a first pass from north to south at about 600 feet and then a series of passes from the four cardinal points, down to about 50 feet, without making out any outline because of the brilliance of the light. The radar operator, whose name is blacked out, tells the same story with other details: the pilot, whom he calls "Martin", was the one who spotted the light; he could not pick it up on his radar, although the controller said he was detecting it on his scope ("I can not understand how GCI was painting this target and I could not pick it up"); they made about seven passes, and when he looked up from the scope it appeared to be "a bright blue light".

The two statements tell what happened next in a different order. According to the operator, after the last pass, at about 7,000 feet, Bromide announced that they had something on their tail; he turned and thought he saw a plane, without being sure, because it lasted a second. According to the pilot, it was the operator who, on the last pass, looked back and said he thought he saw an object on their tail, and he gave it little credence until Bromide called to say it was detecting something behind the fighter on its scope. The pilot asked for an intercept vector and, with the light still in sight, turned to starboard. On a northeasterly heading, the operator locked on to a target with the airborne radar, an APG-33, at 7,000 yards, nearly dead ahead and slightly above, and the fighter began to close at 50 knots faster than the target. At 6,000 yards the target began to pull away. The pilot lit the afterburner, from about 250 knots, and followed the target in a gradual climb, past 10,000 feet, with the pip nearly centred on the scope, while the range opened at a steady rate: to about 26,000 yards in 12 to 15 seconds, according to the pilot, or about 24,000 in about 14, according to the operator. There the lock broke, and they did not pick it up again for the rest of the mission. Neither man saw evasive action or exhaust. The operator added: "I believe that this was the target GCI was painting all the time, and that he was in our area while we were making passes at the light".

The next day the Fifth Air Force intelligence summary recorded the two episodes separately: at 0320, at CT 3930 and 7,500 feet, the radar tail chase of an "unidentified aircraft"; at 0325, at CT 5050 and 7,000 feet, an "unidentified aircraft" with a very strong light, visible from more than 5 miles, which the crew said was "definitely" not a balloon, because they had passed directly beneath it at 50 feet; "No outline was visible because of the brilliant light". Those times reverse the order of the statements, which put the light before the chase. On 29 May both crewmen signed their statements (the pilot's before Captain Fielder C. Slingluff III; in the operator's, the witness's name is blacked out), and on the 31st Captain Vincent A. Goskey, of Detachment 1, 6004th Air Intelligence Service Squadron, sent report 52-85 with the answers to the questionnaire sent by Far East Air Forces (FEAF) intelligence: the radar was checked before and after each mission and was working "very good"; the operator never took his eyes off the scope; the time was measured by counting aloud, with an error the report puts at no more than two seconds a minute. The report also says of the radar target that "no actual ascertainable visual observation was made", and of the light that there was only visual contact. Someone wrote a "?" in the margin beside those two underlined sentences. Page 2 of that four-page report is not in the file, and on pages 7 and 8 of the FEAF extract a hand wrote "Where's the rest of the report?".

Brigadier General Charles Y. Banfill, FEAF Deputy for Intelligence, did the arithmetic: about 68,500 feet covered, an acceleration of 650 feet per second squared, about 20 g, and a final speed of about 5,580 knots; even if the timing or the calibration were off by 50%, it would still exceed any known missile. He added that the Bromide controller had not yet sent anything on the returns he plotted, and concluded that the acceleration led to the belief that the APG-33 was not working properly at the time of contact, despite the checks. The Blue Book record card summarises the case as "Ground Radar, Air Radar, Air Visual Combined Sightings", gives as its solution a possible malfunction of the airborne radar and ticks "Possibly Balloon", with "Was Aircraft", "Probably Aircraft" and "Unknown" crossed out; Blue Book's 1952 index lists it as "BALLOON WITH FLARE".
whyMatters:
El expediente cuenta dos cosas distintas y la tarjeta las mezcla. Su resumen dice que, durante el enganche, el piloto y el operador vieron una luz blanca muy brillante justo delante y que fue esa luz la que se alejó; las declaraciones firmadas y el informe 52-85 dicen otra cosa: la luz fue un primer objeto que el radar de a bordo no captó, aunque el controlador de tierra dijo que lo estaba detectando, y el blanco que se alejó en la pantalla fue un segundo objeto que nadie llegó a ver con claridad.

Leído así, cada parte tiene su explicación propuesta. La luz, sin contorno, a la que pudieron hacer pasadas desde los cuatro puntos cardinales, encaja con los globos con luz que los F-94 derribaron diez días antes en la misma cuadrícula. El mismo legajo trae el parte: un globo de unos 3 pies con «a small light», que subía a 2.000 pies por minuto de 13.000 a 24.000, y otro de 3 a 6 pies cuya luz blanca, «Very powerful», «was still burning as the balloon fell». Al extractarlo, la oficina ATIL de la inteligencia de las FEAF comentó que esos globos podían explicar muchos avistamientos de esa zona de Corea. Eran globos enemigos: el resumen de las FEAF del 13 de junio, titulado «Enemy balloons», cuenta que un observador avanzado vio subir y bajar un globo con un cable junto al frente y apunta que «could possibly be a method of communication». El mismo extracto recoge informes de aviones enemigos con reflectores sobre el noroeste de Corea, aunque ninguno en la cuadrícula CT. La tripulación negó que fuera un globo «as several passes were made directly beneath at 50 ft range».

La parte del radar es la que da peso al caso. Hay un aviso del radar de tierra, un enganche del radar de a bordo con su operador, que firmó lo que vio en la pantalla, y una medida del tiempo que el propio informe explica. La explicación de las FEAF, una avería del APG-33, no está refutada, porque una comprobación antes y después del vuelo no descarta un fallo durante el contacto, pero tampoco explica que Bromide detectara en su pantalla algo en la cola del caza antes del enganche; los datos de ese radar de tierra, que habrían permitido comprobarlo, nunca llegaron al expediente.

El lugar también importa. La tarjeta y el informe 52-85 dicen «North Korea», y las coordenadas se dan en la cuadrícula militar de la época; el oficial que investigó escribió que la luz estaba más allá de la línea de bombardeo y que el blanco rápido estaba «to the rear of our front lines», en territorio que hoy pertenece a Corea del Sur.
whyMatters_en:
The file tells two different things and the record card blends them. Its summary says that, during the lock-on, the pilot and the operator saw a brilliant white light straight ahead and that it was this light that pulled away; the signed statements and report 52-85 say otherwise: the light was a first object that the airborne radar did not pick up, although the ground controller said he was detecting it, and the target that drew away on the scope was a second object that nobody saw clearly.

Read this way, each part has its proposed explanation. The light, with no outline, at which they could make passes from the four cardinal points, fits the lighted balloons that F-94s shot down ten days earlier in the same grid. The same folder carries the report: one balloon of about 3 feet with "a small light", climbing at 2,000 feet a minute from 13,000 to 24,000, and another of 3 to 6 feet whose white light, "Very powerful", "was still burning as the balloon fell". In extracting it, the ATIL Office of FEAF intelligence commented that these balloons could explain many of the sightings over that area of Korea. They were enemy balloons: the FEAF summary of 13 June, headed "Enemy balloons", tells how a forward observer saw a balloon raised and lowered on a cable near the front and notes that it "could possibly be a method of communication". The same extract records reports of enemy aircraft carrying searchlights over northwest Korea, though none in the CT grid. The crew denied it was a balloon "as several passes were made directly beneath at 50 ft range".

The radar part is what gives the case its weight. There is a warning from the ground radar, a lock-on by the airborne radar with its operator, who signed what he saw on the scope, and a timing that the report itself explains. FEAF's explanation, a malfunction of the APG-33, is not refuted, because a check before and after the flight does not rule out a fault during the contact, but it does not explain why Bromide detected something on the fighter's tail on its scope before the lock-on either; the data from that ground radar, which would have allowed a check, never reached the file.

The place matters too. The record card and report 52-85 say "North Korea", and the coordinates are given in the military grid of the period; the investigating officer wrote that the light was beyond the bomb line and the fast target was "to the rear of our front lines", in territory that today belongs to South Korea.
evidence: Declaración del piloto, primer teniente (nombre tachado), 29 de mayo de 1952, copia certificada por el primer teniente Walter W. Jungbluth, con el capitán Fielder C. Slingluff III como testigo: Bromide los mandó a CT 4856; vieron una avioneta bajo los reflectores del frente; luego un objeto brillante al que hicieron pasadas hasta 50 pies sin ver contorno; Bromide «painted an object on my tail»; enganche a 7.000 yardas con rumbo nordeste; de 6.000 a unas 26.000 yardas «in 12-15 seconds»; sin maniobras evasivas ni estela de escape.

Declaración del operador de radar, primer teniente (nombre tachado), 29 de mayo de 1952: no logró captar la luz en su radar aunque el controlador decía detectarla en su pantalla; le pareció «a bright blue light»; tras la última pasada creyó ver un avión «only for a second»; enganche a unas 7.000 yardas y 7.000 pies; de 6.000 a unas 24.000 yardas «in about 14 seconds»; «I believe that this was the target GCI was painting all the time». En esta copia el nombre del testigo está tachado.

Informe AF 112 52-85, Destacamento 1 del 6004.º Escuadrón de Servicio de Inteligencia Aérea, 31 de mayo de 1952, capitán Vincent A. Goskey, aprobado por el coronel Jean H. Daugherty: segundo objeto a las 03:20 I en CT 3930, unos 14 segundos, unos 7.000 pies, cielo «very clear»; radar APG-33 comprobado antes y después de cada misión; tiempo medido contando en voz alta; «No actual ascertainable visual observation was made». Del primer objeto: «Only a visual contact was made. Unable to contact with radar». Falta la página 2 de 4.

Comentario del oficial que investigó, en el mismo informe: los dos objetos pudieron estar relacionados; la luz estaba más allá de la línea de bombardeo y el objeto rápido, detrás de las líneas propias.

Comentario del general de brigada Charles Y. Banfill, responsable de inteligencia de las FEAF (Deputy for Intelligence): unos 68.500 pies, 650 pies/s² (unas 20 g), velocidad final de unos 5.580 nudos; sin datos todavía del controlador de Bromide; «The phenomenal acceleration reported leads to the belief that the APG-33 was not operating correctly at the time of contact, despite checks before and after the mission».

Resumen de inteligencia de la Quinta Fuerza Aérea del 27 de mayo, extractado en el informe IR-23-52 de la oficina ATIL de las FEAF: persecución por radar a las 03:20 I en CT 3930 a 7.500 pies (comentario: velocidad final de unos 3.000 mph si el informe es exacto) y luz muy fuerte a las 03:25 I en CT 5050 a 7.000 pies, que la tripulación dio por «definitely not a balloon» porque pasaron justo por debajo a 50 pies, con «No outline was visible because of the brilliant light»; comentario de la oficina ATIL: informes de aviones enemigos con reflectores en el noroeste de Corea, «though none have been reported in the CT area».

Mismo informe IR-23-52, extracto del resumen del 19 de mayo: el 16 de mayo, a las 02:10 y 03:53 I, tripulaciones de F-94 siguieron y derribaron en la cuadrícula CT un globo de unos 3 pies con una luz pequeña, que subía a 2.000 pies por minuto de 13.000 a 24.000 pies, y otro de 3 a 6 pies a 12.000 pies cuya luz blanca, «Very powerful», «was still burning as the balloon fell»; comentario de la oficina ATIL: «This report of lighted balloons may be a basis of explanation for many of the sightings reported over this area of Korea».

Mismo informe IR-23-52, extracto del resumen de inteligencia de las FEAF n.º 717 del 13 de junio de 1952, titulado «Enemy balloons»: luces que cambiaban de color junto al frente en mayo y junio; un observador avanzado vio un globo «being raised and lowered on a cable»; comentario: «could possibly be a method of communication».

Tarjeta de Blue Book: 26 de mayo de 1952, 03:20 I, «North Korea», radar de tierra, radar aéreo y visual desde el aire, 2 objetos, 14 segundos; solución: «Possible malfunction of airborne radar set»; marca «Possibly Balloon», con «Was Aircraft», «Probably Aircraft» y «Unknown» tachados. Su resumen dice que los dos tripulantes vieron la luz durante el enganche, lo que contradice el informe 52-85.
Índice de Blue Book de 1952, avistamientos del 11 al 31 de mayo: «26 North Korea Military (RADAR) BALLOON WITH FLARE».
evidence_en: Statement of the pilot, first lieutenant (name blacked out), 29 May 1952, true copy certified by First Lieutenant Walter W. Jungbluth, with Captain Fielder C. Slingluff III as witness: Bromide sent them to CT 4856; they saw a small plane under the front-line searchlights; then a brilliant object on which they made passes down to 50 feet without seeing an outline; Bromide "painted an object on my tail"; lock-on at 7,000 yards on a northeasterly heading; from 6,000 to about 26,000 yards "in 12-15 seconds"; no evasive action and no exhaust.

Statement of the radar observer, first lieutenant (name blacked out), 29 May 1952: he could not pick up the light on his radar although the controller said he was painting it; it appeared to be "a bright blue light"; after the last pass he thought he saw a plane "only for a second"; lock-on at about 7,000 yards and 7,000 feet; from 6,000 to about 24,000 yards "in about 14 seconds"; "I believe that this was the target GCI was painting all the time". In this copy the witness's name is blacked out.

AF Form 112 report 52-85, Detachment 1, 6004th Air Intelligence Service Squadron, 31 May 1952, Captain Vincent A. Goskey, approved by Colonel Jean H. Daugherty: second object at 0320 I at CT 3930, about 14 seconds, about 7,000 feet, "very clear"; APG-33 radar checked before and after each mission; time measured by counting aloud; "No actual ascertainable visual observation was made". On the first object: "Only a visual contact was made. Unable to contact with radar". Page 2 of 4 is missing.
Comment of the investigating officer, in the same report: the two objects might have been related; the light was beyond the bomb line and the fast object behind friendly lines.

Comment of Brigadier General Charles Y. Banfill, FEAF Deputy for Intelligence: about 68,500 feet, 650 ft/s² (about 20 g), final speed about 5,580 knots; no data yet from the Bromide controller; "The phenomenal acceleration reported leads to the belief that the APG-33 was not operating correctly at the time of contact, despite checks before and after the mission".

Fifth Air Force intelligence summary of 27 May, extracted in report IR-23-52 of the FEAF ATIL Office: radar tail chase at 0320 I at CT 3930 at 7,500 feet (comment: final speed of about 3,000 mph if accurate) and a very strong light at 0325 I at CT 5050 at 7,000 feet, which the crew called "definitely not a balloon" because they passed directly beneath it at 50 feet, with "No outline was visible because of the brilliant light"; ATIL Office comment: reports of enemy aircraft carrying searchlights over northwest Korea, "though none have been reported in the CT area".

Same report IR-23-52, extract of the 19 May summary: on 16 May, at 0210 and 0353 I, F-94 crews chased and shot down in the CT grid one balloon of about 3 feet with a small light, climbing at 2,000 feet a minute from 13,000 to 24,000 feet, and another of 3 to 6 feet at 12,000 feet whose white light, "Very powerful", "was still burning as the balloon fell"; ATIL Office comment: "This report of lighted balloons may be a basis of explanation for many of the sightings reported over this area of Korea".

Same report IR-23-52, extract of FEAF intelligence summary no. 717 of 13 June 1952, headed "Enemy balloons": lights changing colour near the front in May and June; a forward observer saw a balloon "being raised and lowered on a cable"; comment: "could possibly be a method of communication".

Blue Book record card: 26 May 1952, 0320 I, "North Korea", ground radar, aerial radar and air visual, 2 objects, 14 seconds; solution: "Possible malfunction of airborne radar set"; ticks "Possibly Balloon", with "Was Aircraft", "Probably Aircraft" and "Unknown" crossed out. Its summary says both crewmen saw the light during the lock-on, which contradicts report 52-85.
Blue Book's 1952 index, sightings of 11 to 31 May: "26 North Korea Military (RADAR) BALLOON WITH FLARE".

classBasis.es: El general de brigada Charles Y. Banfill, responsable de inteligencia de las FEAF (Deputy for Intelligence), concluyó en el informe 52-85: «The phenomenal acceleration reported leads to the belief that the APG-33 was not operating correctly at the time of contact, despite checks before and after the mission», y la tarjeta de Blue Book da como solución «Possible malfunction of airborne radar set». La propuesta es débil y está en disputa, no refutada: la tripulación declaró que el radar se comprobó antes y después y funcionaba bien, lo que no excluye un fallo durante el contacto, pero la avería del radar de a bordo no explica que el radar de tierra señalara un blanco en la cola del caza antes del enganche, y los datos de ese radar nunca llegaron al expediente. La clase cubre solo la capa del radar. La luz a la que hicieron las pasadas tiene otra propuesta, de clase aeronave: la tarjeta marca «Possibly Balloon» y el índice de Blue Book, «BALLOON WITH FLARE», en una cuadrícula donde los F-94 habían derribado globos con luz diez días antes; la oficina ATIL de la inteligencia de las FEAF comentó que esos globos podían explicar muchos avistamientos de la zona, y el resumen de las FEAF del 13 de junio los trata como «Enemy balloons», alzados junto al frente quizá como «a method of communication». El mismo extracto menciona aviones enemigos con reflectores en el noroeste de Corea, «though none have been reported in the CT area». La tripulación negó que fuera un globo «as several passes were made directly beneath at 50 ft range»; no vio contorno «because of the brilliant light».
classBasis.en: Brigadier General Charles Y. Banfill, FEAF Deputy for Intelligence, concluded in report 52-85: "The phenomenal acceleration reported leads to the belief that the APG-33 was not operating correctly at the time of contact, despite checks before and after the mission", and the Blue Book record card gives as its solution "Possible malfunction of airborne radar set". The proposal is weak and disputed, not refuted: the crew stated that the radar was checked before and after and worked well, which does not exclude a fault during the contact, but a malfunction of the airborne radar does not explain why the ground radar reported a target on the fighter's tail before the lock-on, and that radar's data never reached the file. The class covers only the radar layer. The light the crew made passes at has another proposal, of the aircraft class: the card ticks "Possibly Balloon" and Blue Book's index says "BALLOON WITH FLARE", in a grid where F-94s had shot down lighted balloons ten days earlier; the ATIL Office of FEAF intelligence commented that these balloons could explain many sightings in the area, and the FEAF summary of 13 June treats them as "Enemy balloons", raised near the front perhaps as "a method of communication". The same extract mentions enemy aircraft carrying searchlights over northwest Korea, "though none have been reported in the CT area". The crew denied it was a balloon "as several passes were made directly beneath at 50 ft range"; they saw no outline "because of the brilliant light".
